header:
Date: 2026-05-22
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood CSM); Jake Moreno (Orion Head of ML), Priya Singh (Infra), Samir Ahmad (Security), Tess Wu (Product)
summary: Initial discovery for Dedicated capacity: customer wants isolated reserved GPUs for PHI processing, needs aggressive burst behavior for daytime traffic spikes, and must meet SOC2-like audit/KMS controls. Key concerns: cost of always-on pools, predictable failover to hosted without data leakage, and integration with existing VPC/KMS. Agreed next: pricing + capacity worksheet, security docs, pilot kickoff.
topics: Dedicated reservation sizing, isolation and tenancy (single-tenant node vs tenant pools), burst credits and graceful degradation, fallback routing to Hosted API, KV cache and prefix caching strategies, monitoring and alerting needs (per-route latency/tokens), compliance (SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS) and network egress
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I think we have about 50 minutes, quick intros?
[00:06] Jake Moreno: Yeah hi I'm Jake, head of ML at Orion Health, we run several clinical NLP pipelines and are looking at options for inference — we need to keep PHI on private infra, but want the Redwood experience.
[00:16] Priya Singh: Priya, infra eng, I manage k8s on-prem and cloud networking.
[00:21] Samir Ahmad: Samir, security, SOC two and audit point person.
[00:25] Tess Wu: Tess, product, I'll own success metrics.
[00:28] Maya Chen: Great, I'm Maya AE and with Ravi, our solutions engineer, and Lena on CSM. Ravi?
[00:33] Ravi Patel: Hi all, quick overview: Redwood Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools, isolation options (VPC/private nodes), and burst capacity. I'll try to map to your workloads and constraints.
[00:43] [00:45] Jake Moreno: Quick context — we have steady base inference of about 250 qps overnight and daytime spikes up to 1.8k qps across many short prompts (EHR summarization). Latency target is p95 < 250ms for user-facing flows, and cost is obviously a factor. We process PHI so Private or Dedicated with VPC needed, not hosted public.
[01:12] Maya Chen: Understood. Do you have an initial budget or procurement window?
[01:16] Tess Wu: We're in budgeting for H2, pilot in June would be ideal, procurement in July. Budget is flexible but we want hard unit economics before committing.
[01:27] [01:30] Priya Singh: On infra: we prefer single-tenant isolation for PHI workloads, but we also want to allow bursts to spill into shared capacity during extreme peaks. How does Redwood handle that without leaking data?
[01:42] Ravi Patel: Good question — we have Private deployments (customer-managed control plane) and Dedicated (Redwood-managed but isolated GPU pools). For Dedicated we can provision node affinity to your tenant; for spillover we can route to compatible model variants on Redwood-hosted endpoints with encryption in transit and ephemeral caching, but we treat PHI differently — if data residency prohibits spill to hosted, we keep everything in your VPC. There are tradeoffs: guaranteed capacity vs cost efficiency.
[02:12] Samir Ahmad: We cannot allow PHI to go to any multi-tenant environment. So the spillover to hosted is a no-go unless we strip PHI or tokenization occurs upstream.
[02:23] Ravi Patel: Totally — then we'd configure a strict policy: no external fallback for PHI routes, instead we'll use reserved burst pool and queue/scale. For burst surfacing beyond reserved we can provide a preapproved isolated burst buffer (reserved warm nodes) — it's more costly but keeps data in your tenancy.
[02:42] [02:45] Jake Moreno: Can you explain burst credits or burst model more concretely? We can't keep capacity at peak 24/7.
[02:52] Maya Chen: Sure — two approaches: conservative reserved pool sized to expected base traffic plus a smaller warm reserve for spikes, or reserved baseline with automated horizontal scaling and short-term burst credits which you pay for when used. We also have scheduled scaling windows for known peak hours.
[03:11] Ravi Patel: Technically we keep a hot w/kv cache on GPU, so cold starts are expensive. Our runtime offers prewarmed instances and KV/prefix caching to reduce token cost for repeated patterns. But prewarmed reserved GPUs cost you steady dollars.
[03:27] [03:30] Priya Singh: We're interested in quantization too — does Redwood recommend 4-bit models to reduce GPU memory? We run clinical models where slight quality loss is tolerable for some non-critical flows.
[03:40] Ravi Patel: Yes, we can run int4/4-bit quantized weights; we also recommend validating with your prompts. We can provide a quality regression harness as part of the pilot to show p95/p99 deltas.
[03:53] [04:00] Tess Wu: Who from our side will need to be involved for SOC2 sign-off? Samir will lead, but Priya will own network.
[04:08] Samir Ahmad: We'll need KMS integration (customer-managed keys), audit logs with retention for 2 years, SSO/SAML for RBAC, and the ability to run penetration tests. Does Redwood Support customer-managed KMS for Dedicated/Private?
[04:22] Ravi Patel: For Private yes, for Dedicated we have KMS integrations (bring your own keys) in our enterprise plan. Audit logs and fine-grained RBAC are available; we'll share SOC2 cert and our pen test policy.
[04:36] [04:40] Jake Moreno: Latency expectations — you mentioned p95 < 250ms, is that realistically achievable for our long prompts?
[04:46] Ravi Patel: Depends on sequence lengths. For shorter prompts and optimized batching, yes. For long clinical notes (>2k tokens) we recommend model sharding/long context kernels, and latency will be higher. We can profile with a small trace of your workload.
[05:03] [05:15] Maya Chen: Also worth discussing graceful degradation: if the reserved pool saturates, do you want requests queued, reject with 429, or fall back to a lower-cost/latency-optimized model variant?
[05:24] Tess Wu: Prefer degrade to a lighter model for non-critical flows, but not for PHI. For PHI, queueing is fine as long as SLA is communicated.
[05:35] Priya Singh: What about Kubernetes-level isolation? We run EKS; can Redwood Dedicated integrate with our VPC and peering?
[05:43] Ravi Patel: Yes, we support VPC peering and private link depending on cloud. For on-prem we offer Private deployment. For EKS we can provide an agent for secure routing or use ILB endpoints. We'll map network egress and IP allowlists.
[05:58] [06:00] Jake Moreno: A practical question: during spikes we have a lot of short requests (many at once). Does Redwood support microburst handling or do you batch aggressively which can increase latency?
[06:10] Ravi Patel: Our continuous batching runtime groups small requests to GPUs to increase throughput while respecting latency SLOs. We tune batching windows per-route. For microbursts, we recommend a combination of small reserved concurrency and per-route burst tokens — this avoids excessive batching delays.
[06:27] [06:30] Maya Chen: We should talk numbers — what's a typical reserved GPU count mapping to qps for say a 70B model quantized to int8? Ravi?
[06:38] Ravi Patel: Very rough: one A100-like equivalent can handle ~200-400 short prompt qps for quantized 70B depending on sequence length and batching. For your daytime peak 1.8k qps you'd look at 5–10 GPUs depending on batching profiles and whether you shard. We'll put real numbers in the sizing doc.
[06:55] [07:00] Priya Singh: What's the failover pattern if a node fails? Do requests get retried on another GPU or requeued?
[07:06] Ravi Patel: Failed requests are retried with exponential backoff; we also keep proactive warmers and automatic replacement. For strict latency SLOs we recommend cross-zone capacity.
[07:18] [07:30] Samir Ahmad: On compliance — our auditors will ask for separation of logs and proof that only authorized principals can decrypt PHI. Can Redwood provide per-tenant logging and KMS audit trails?
[07:40] Ravi Patel: Yes, we can supply isolated audit streams and KMS usage logs. For Dedicated, we can integrate with your cloud KMS; for Private, keys stay in your environment.
[07:51] [08:00] Tess Wu: Cost question: what are typical costs for reserved vs burst? We want an apples-to-apples comparison with an on-prem Triton stack.
[08:09] Maya Chen: We'll share a worksheet with reserved hourly rates, expected utilization, and burst chargebacks. High-level: reserved lowers per-token cost but raises base spend; burst is pay-as-you-go and can spike costs. On-prem has a higher ops burden.
[08:27] [08:30] Jake Moreno: Can you do a hybrid: reserved for PHI routes and hosted for non-PHI?
[08:34] Ravi Patel: Absolutely. We commonly advise splitting routes. We'll tag routes as PHI and route them to Dedicated/Private, while public traffic uses hosted endpoints.
[08:44] [09:00] Priya Singh: Network egress — our cloud provider charges high egress. If Redwood Dedicated is in your managed cloud, will we incur egress charges?
[09:07] Ravi Patel: If Dedicated runs in a region under Redwood-managed infra and you peer, egress is subject to cloud provider billing. We can discuss colocated deployment options to minimize egress or Private deployment where traffic stays in your VPC.
[09:22] [09:30] Maya Chen: Let's capture risk appetite: immediate pilot should include non-PHI flows to validate perf, and a parallel security validation for PHI configuration. Agree?
[09:36] Jake Moreno: Yes agreed, but we want a short PHI smoke test in staging with zero-hosted fallback.
[09:42] Ravi Patel: That's doable — set up isolated pilot cluster with KMS. We'll provide an eval checklist.
[09:49] [10:00] Tess Wu: On monitoring — we need per-route token counts, cost attribution, and latency histograms. Is that in Console?
[10:08] Ravi Patel: Yes, Redwood Console provides token-level costs, per-route dashboards, and tracing. We can add custom alerts and retention windows.
[10:17] [10:30] Priya Singh: Any limitations on containerized telemetry going into our Splunk/Datadog?
[10:34] Ravi Patel: We have integrations and can forward logs to your endpoints; for sensitive logs we can limit PII in forwarded streams.
[10:42] [11:00] Maya Chen: Objection we hear often: "Why not just run Triton on our cluster?" How would you respond?
[11:09] Jake Moreno: (laughs) We actually considered that.
[11:12] Ravi Patel: Triton gives control but you get ops burden — kernel tune, batching, quantization engineering, and serving runtime optimizations. Redwood offers the runtime plus orchestration, rollouts, tracing, and a SRE-backed SLA. We can often beat self-hosted TCO when you factor in engineering time.
[11:31] [11:40] Samir Ahmad: What's the SLA for Dedicated?
[11:43] Maya Chen: We offer SLA-backed uptime and latency objectives on enterprise plan, will include in pricing.
[11:49] [12:00] Tess Wu: For the pilot, can we get 2–3 reserved GPUs and the ability to burst to 8 for 2 hours/day?
[12:08] Ravi Patel: Yes, that's a typical pilot. We'll define burst guardrails and simulate peak traffic to measure.
[12:18] [12:30] Priya Singh: Any preemption risk? We can't have preemptible nodes for PHI.
[12:34] Ravi Patel: No preemptible instances for reserved Dedicated nodes; those are guaranteed. Burst pools can be preemptible in the optional cheaper tier, but we'll mark PHI buckets as non-preemptible.
[12:47] [13:00] Jake Moreno: What's the onboarding timeline and who will own it?
[13:04] Lena Ortiz: CSM here — onboarding for pilot usually 2–3 weeks with an SE and an onboarding engineer. We'll provide a runbook and weekly check-ins.
[13:15] [13:30] Tess Wu: Success metrics: p95 latency under 250ms for user flows, PHI requests never leave our tenancy, cost per 1M tokens under target X (will share).
[13:40] [13:45] Maya Chen: We'll need your token profile and a small corpus to run regressions.
[13:49] Jake Moreno: We'll redact PHI for the initial perf runs but provide a PHI-enabled staging later.
[13:55] [14:00] Priya Singh: Can we talk about KV cache behavior — does cache persist across warmers or is it ephemeral per node?
[14:08] Ravi Patel: KV cache is per process but we support prefix caching and cross-request KV replication strategies that keep hot contexts available. In Dedicated you can have persistent caches on warm nodes. We'll show cache hit rates from our benchmarks.
[14:25] [14:30] Tess Wu: Any limits on model uploads or private model hosting? We plan to use a fine-tuned clinical model.
[14:39] Ravi Patel: You can bring your own models; we'll help onboard and version. Private model hosting under Dedicated is supported. We also provide model variant rollouts.
[14:52] [15:00] Maya Chen: Let's capture the blockers — Samir?
[15:03] Samir Ahmad: Main blocker is legal: we need DPA changes for PHI, plus proof of KMS separation. Also need network diagram.
[15:11] Maya Chen: We'll provide SOC2 and KMS docs. Lena will coordinate with legal.
[15:16] [15:30] Jake Moreno: Anything else on the technical side?
[15:21] Priya Singh: I'd like to see a latency profile for both quantized and full precision models under our token distribution.
[15:26] Ravi Patel: We'll include that in the sizing doc and run a short benchmark with your sample traces.
[15:34] [16:00] Tess Wu: Ok last: procurement — what contract length options?
[16:08] Maya Chen: Monthly reserved and annual committed plans; discounts for 12+ month commitments. We'll include an example contract.
[16:15] [16:30] Jake Moreno: Sounds good.
[16:18] Maya Chen: Great — quick recap of next steps: Maya sends pricing + contract sketches and burst worksheet; Ravi sends capacity sizing and benchmarking plan; Lena schedules pilot kickoff for June 2; Samir gets SOC2 + network diagram to us.
[16:34] [16:40] Samir Ahmad: I'll share network doc by 5/26.
[16:36] Priya Singh: I'll prepare token distribution and a small trace file; redacted for PHI for now.
[16:41] Maya Chen: Perfect. Thank you all.
[16:44] Jake Moreno: Thanks everyone.
[16:48] [16:50] Meeting ends.
questions: Can Redwood guarantee no PHI leaves the tenant during burst?
What's the expected qps per A100-equivalent for quantized 70B?
How do burst credits get billed and can they be budget-capped?
